ukmt-cayley-2026-c1.prompt:
Cayley, Hamilton and Maclaurin each have an amount of money.

If Cayley gave Hamilton 1 pound then Hamilton would have three times the amount that Cayley would have.

If instead Hamilton gave Maclaurin 1 pound then Maclaurin would have twice the amount that Hamilton would have.

If instead Maclaurin gave Cayley 1 pound then Cayley would have a quarter of the amount that Maclaurin would have.

If instead Cayley and Hamilton each gave Maclaurin 1 pound, how many times the total of Cayley and Hamilton will Maclaurin have?

ukmt-cayley-2026-c2.prompt:
A $3\times3$ grid has the middle square shaded out. The digits $1$ to $8$ are placed in the grid once each to form four three-digit numbers, two reading left-to-right and two reading top-to-bottom, in such a way that all the three-digit numbers are multiples of $4$.

Find how many ways this can be done.

ukmt-cayley-2026-c3.prompt:
$BCDF$ is a rhombus with side length $x$. $E$ lies on $DF$ and $ABCE$ is a parallelogram. $AB$ has length $y$ and $AF$ has length $z$. The perimeter of trapezium $ABCD$ is $10\%$ more than the perimeter of $BCDF$. The perimeter of $ABCE$ is $10\%$ less than the perimeter of $BCDF$.

Prove that $ABCE$ is, in fact, a rectangle.
ukmt-cayley-2026-c3.answer: The perimeter conditions give $y=0.8x$ and $z=0.6x$, so $y^2+z^2=x^2$ and triangle $ABF$ is right-angled at $A$; hence the parallelogram $ABCE$ has a right angle.

ukmt-cayley-2026-c4.prompt:
$D$ is a point on the side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$ such that $AB=AD=CD=2BD$. $F$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ respectively, so that $FE$ is parallel to $BC$.

Prove that triangle $DEF$ is isosceles.
ukmt-cayley-2026-c4.answer: With $\angle ACB=\theta$, angle chasing gives $\angle DEF=\angle DFE=90^\circ-\theta$, so $DE=DF$.

ukmt-cayley-2026-c5.prompt:
On an ordinary clock-face the numbers in adjacent positions always differ by either $1$ or $11$.

Is it possible to re-arrange the numbers $1$ to $12$ round the clock-face so that the two numbers in adjacent positions always differ by $3$, $4$, or $5$?

ukmt-cayley-2026-c6.prompt:
Find all triples of distinct primes $(p,q,r)$ satisfying the equation below.
$$(p-5)(q-21)(r-26)=pqr$$
